The [ASCII Table Reference](/ascii-table-reference) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Every ASCII character 0–127 with decimal, hex and name. Enter your search and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Every ASCII character from 0 to 127 with its decimal code, hexadecimal code, character and name — control characters (NUL, TAB, LF, ESC and the rest), punctuation, digits, upper- and lower-case letters, and DEL. Search by character, name or number to find a code in seconds. It is a reference, not a calculator: the table is fixed, so there is nothing to calculate. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the ASCII Table Reference

Start by typing or pasting your search. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. When you want a clean slate, Reset restores the defaults. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Scroll the table or type in the search box to filter it.
2. Read the decimal and hex codes for any character.
3. Use the codes in your code or documents wherever a character code is needed.

## How it works

The [ASCII Table Reference](/ascii-table-reference) works straight from the values you enter: change an input and the result updates immediately, with no page reload and no waiting. Everything happens in your browser, so your entries never leave your device. Try it with a few different values and you will quickly get a feel for how the inputs move the result.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. The letter A is decimal 65 (hex 41); a newline (LF) is decimal 10; the space character is decimal 32. Try the same figures in the [ASCII Table Reference](/ascii-table-reference) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves. The steps are the same whatever numbers you use; only the figures change.

## Trying it out

The fastest way to see what the [ASCII Table Reference](/ascii-table-reference) does is to open it and enter values you already know the answer for. Change one input at a time and watch how the result responds — that tells you more than any description. Everything runs in your browser, so you can experiment freely: nothing is saved, sent or tracked.

## What ASCII is

ASCII is the original 7-bit character set: 128 characters, each with a number from 0 to 127. The first 32 are control characters (things like TAB, LF for newline, and ESC), 32 is the space, 48–57 are the digits, 65–90 are A–Z, 97–122 are a–z, and 127 is DEL. Everything beyond 127 is not ASCII — it belongs to other encodings such as UTF-8.

## Why the codes matter

Character codes show up in programming (for example, checking whether a key press is Enter, code 13), in URLs and data formats (percent-encoding uses hex codes), and in old file formats. Knowing that A is 65 and a is 97 explains why sorting is case-sensitive in most systems.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Search for a name like TAB or a number like 65 to jump straight to it.
- Control characters 0–31 do not print — their names are shown instead.
- Hex codes are the same numbers in base 16, used in URLs and colour codes.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is ASCII?

A 7-bit character set with 128 characters — control characters, punctuation, digits and letters — each with a number from 0 to 127. It is the basis of text in computing. Try it with your own numbers in the [ASCII Table Reference](/ascii-table-reference) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the ASCII code for A?

65 in decimal, 41 in hexadecimal. Lowercase a is 97 (61 in hex). Try it with your own numbers in the [ASCII Table Reference](/ascii-table-reference) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Why are there control characters?

The first 32 codes control devices and text flow rather than printing a character — TAB moves to the next tab stop, LF starts a new line, ESC starts an escape sequence. Try it with your own numbers in the [ASCII Table Reference](/ascii-table-reference) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What do I need to use the ASCII Table Reference?

Just Search. Enter those values and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. If you are unsure about a value, try a rough figure first and then refine it — the result updates instantly.
